evidence: Each use case class (AssignTaskUseCase, CreateProjectUseCase, CreateTaskUseCase, CreateUserUseCase, ListProjectTasksUseCase, MarkTaskDoneUseCase) has a single execute(input) method and returns a DTO from dto.ts (toTaskDto, toProjectDto, toUserDto).
CreateProjectUseCase, CreateTaskUseCase and CreateUserUseCase all get IDs through the IdGenerator port, which they receive in their constructors (IdGenerator.ts: next(): string).
Domain changes go through domain methods: task.assignTo in AssignTaskUseCase.ts, task.markDone in MarkTaskDoneUseCase.ts, Task.create in CreateTaskUseCase.ts.
Status validity uses the domain helper isTaskStatus (ListProjectTasksUseCase.ts), not a local copy of the status list.
Minor repetition: the task-belongs-to-project guard appears in both AssignTaskUseCase.execute and MarkTaskDoneUseCase.execute. It is a short lookup guard, not a domain rule that has been duplicated.

It gets domain repositories and the IdGenerator port through its constructor, has one execute(input) method, calls the domain (Task.create, task.assignTo, task.markDone, Project.create, User.create), saves, and returns a DTO through dto.ts. No use case builds a DTO by hand or creates IDs without IdGenerator, so none of them skips the module's own abstractions. Business rules stay in the domain. Status validity comes from isTaskStatus in the domain, and Task.create receives the raw status. parseDueDate is input parsing at the edge of the use case and lives only in CreateTaskUseCase. One guard is repeated: the check that a task belongs to the given project ('!task || task.projectId !== input.projectId') appears in both AssignTaskUseCase and MarkTaskDoneUseCase. Some existence checks also repeat across use cases. These are short lookup guards, not domain rules that are re-implemented or could drift apart in a meaningful way. They could be pulled into a helper, but they don't count as a split concern or a broken boundary under this rubric.
